notes.title: Start here: a bank simulator in three layers
notes.body:
This is a terminal bank: create accounts, deposit, withdraw, transfer, and read each account's history. Everything is stored in two text files under `data/`.

The code has three layers plus models:

- **App.java** - the menu. It reads text, calls the service, prints results, and saves.
- **service/BankService.java** - every banking rule: which accounts exist, which amounts are allowed, and which records a change creates.
- **storage/FileStorage.java** - turning accounts and transactions into lines and back.
- **model/** - `BankAccount`, `Transaction` and the `TransactionType` enum hold data and do no checking.

The README walks through each method and each money flow. Read it beside the code, and when the two differ, believe the code.

To run it, compile all files under `src` into `out` (the README has a PowerShell line; on Git Bash, `javac -d out $(find src -name "*.java")` works) and run `java -cp out bankapp.App` from a scratch folder. Account ids are long UUIDs, so copy them from the "Account ID:" line.

excerpts.quote: This structure teaches an important beginner lesson: different code should have different jobs.

readMore.why: One entry per method, then the deposit, withdrawal and transfer flows.

notes.title: Concept: from typed text to a two-decimal amount
notes.body:
Money is `BigDecimal` everywhere, never `double` (the README explains why). An amount passes through two steps before it touches a balance, and both are worth reading slowly.

1. **Parsing, in App.readAmount.** The typed text goes straight into `new BigDecimal(String)`. Look up that constructor's documentation and list which spellings of a number it accepts. Note which exception it throws for text it rejects, and what `readAmount` turns that into.
2. **Cleaning, in BankService.validateAmount.** Note the two arguments passed to `setScale`, and read the documentation of that rounding mode. Then note whether the "greater than zero" comparison looks at the typed amount or at the rounded one.

Work a few amounts through both steps on paper (a whole number, one with three decimals, a very small one), then run the app and compare. The `toPlainString` calls in `App` decide how the result is printed.

excerpts.quote: `double` uses binary floating-point math, which can create tiny rounding errors.

readMore.why: readAmount and the four money actions that call it.

notes.title: Concept: one gate for rules, two files for state
notes.body:
Every change goes through a `BankService` method that checks first and changes second. A check that fails throws an exception, and `App.run` turns `IllegalArgumentException` and `IllegalStateException` into an "Operation failed:" line.

Trace these yourself:

- For `deposit`, `withdraw` and `transfer`, write down every check in the order the code runs it, and the exact comparison each one uses.
- Note which prompts `App` shows before it calls the service at all.
- Find every call to `saveData` in `App`, and note what has already happened when each one runs.
- In `FileStorage.loadAccounts`, see where each field of a `BankAccount` comes from, and look for any code that relates balances to transactions.
- Read `escape` and `splitLine` together and run a few awkward strings through them by hand.
- Note which exceptions `main` catches, and which ones the loaders can throw.

notes.title: Why 10.005 is recorded as 10.01
notes.body:
`validateAmount` calls `amount.setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP)`. Scale 2 keeps two digits after the point, and `HALF_UP` rounds a dropped digit of 5 or more upward, so 10.005 becomes **10.01**. That rounded value is what `deposit` adds to the balance and puts on the transaction.

- *10.005 kept*: `BigDecimal` would keep it, but the service replaces the amount with the scaled one first.
- *10.00, cut off*: that is `RoundingMode.DOWN`, not `HALF_UP`.
- *Refused for extra decimals*: no check counts decimals; the amount is rounded instead.

notes.title: Why 0.004 is refused as not above zero
notes.body:
Rounding happens before the zero check. `setScale(2, HALF_UP)` turns 0.004 into 0.00, because the dropped digit 4 is below 5. Then `cleanAmount.compareTo(ZERO) <= 0` is true and the method throws `IllegalArgumentException("Deposit amount must be greater than zero.")`, which `run()` prints after **"Operation failed: "**.

- *Balance grows by 0.004*: the unrounded value is never used.
- *Recorded as 0.01*: half-up only rounds up from a 5.
- *Not a valid number*: 0.004 parses fine; that message is only for text `BigDecimal` rejects.

excerpts.quote: if (cleanAmount.compareTo(ZERO) <= 0) { throw new IllegalArgumentException(actionName + " amount must be greater than zero.");

notes.title: Why 1e3 deposits a thousand
notes.body:
`readAmount` hands the trimmed text to `new BigDecimal(amountText)`. That constructor accepts scientific notation, so `1e3` means 1 times 10 to the 3rd, stored as `1E+3`. `validateAmount` scales it to **1000.00**, and the deposit goes through. `toPlainString` prints it without the exponent.

- *"Please enter a valid number"*: that is only thrown when the constructor raises `NumberFormatException`, and it does not here.
- *1.00, rest ignored*: the constructor parses the whole string or fails; it never stops early.
- *13.00, e skipped*: no code removes characters from the input.

excerpts.quote: return new BigDecimal(amountText); } catch (NumberFormatException exception) { throw new IllegalArgumentException("Please enter a valid number for the amount.");

notes.title: Why the bad account id is reported last
notes.body:
`App.deposit` only collects input: the id, then the amount through `readAmount`, then the description. Only after all three does it call `bankService.deposit`, and the first thing that does is `requireAccount`, which throws **"Account not found: NOPE"**. So the user types everything before learning the id was wrong.

- *Right after the ID*: `App` never looks the id up itself.
- *Opens an account NOPE*: only `createAccount` adds accounts, with a generated `ACC-` id.
- *Skips the description*: the prompts are fixed; nothing between them checks the id.

(A bad amount is caught earlier, inside `readAmount`, before the description prompt.)

excerpts.quote: String description = scanner.nextLine(); bankService.deposit(accountId, amount, description);
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Account not found: " + accountId);

notes.title: Why the same-account check wins over not-found
notes.body:
`transfer` checks in this order: both ids non-null, then `fromAccountId.equals(toAccountId)`, and only then `requireAccount` for each side. With ZZ on both sides the second check already fails, so the user sees **"You cannot transfer money to the same account."** even though ZZ does not exist.

- *"Account not found: ZZ"*: that comes from `requireAccount`, which runs after the equality check.
- *Insufficient balance*: the balance is checked last of all.
- *Ids are required*: that is only for null ids, and `App` always passes the typed strings.

The README transfer flow lists "checks that both ids exist" before "rejects transfers to the same account". The code does it the other way round.

excerpts.quote: if (fromAccountId.equals(toAccountId)) { throw new IllegalArgumentException("You cannot transfer money to the same account."); } BankAccount sourceAccount = requireAccount(fromAccountId);

notes.title: Why withdrawing the whole balance is allowed
notes.body:
`withdraw` refuses only when `account.getBalance().compareTo(cleanAmount) < 0`, that is, when the balance is strictly smaller than the amount. 30.00 compared with 30.00 gives 0, which is not below 0, so the withdrawal **succeeds** and `decreaseBalance` leaves 0.00.

- *Balance must stay above zero*: the rule only forbids going negative; zero is fine.
- *"Insufficient balance"*: thrown only for a strictly smaller balance.
- *Account closed*: no code removes an account from `accountsById`.

excerpts.quote: if (account.getBalance().compareTo(cleanAmount) < 0) { throw new IllegalStateException("Insufficient balance for this withdrawal."); }

notes.title: What one side of a transfer looks like
notes.body:
`transfer` creates two `Transaction` objects: a `TRANSFER_OUT` on the source, whose `relatedAccountId` is the destination, and a `TRANSFER_IN` on the destination pointing back at the source. Both carry the same positive amount and description. `getTransactionsForAccount(A)` keeps only records whose `accountId` is A, so A sees **one TRANSFER_OUT of $20.00, Related Account B, Description rent**.

- *Both records under A*: the `TRANSFER_IN` belongs to B's account id.
- *A WITHDRAWAL*: transfers use their own two enum values.
- *TRANSFER of -$20.00*: there is no plain TRANSFER type, and amounts are never stored negative; the type carries the direction.

excerpts.quote: Transaction transferOut = createTransaction( sourceAccount.getId(), TransactionType.TRANSFER_OUT, cleanAmount, description, destinationAccount.getId() );

notes.title: Why the deposit survives the crash
notes.body:
`App.deposit` calls `saveData()` immediately after `bankService.deposit` returns, and `saveData` rewrites both files. So the deposit is **on disk before the menu is shown again**. When input then ends, `scanner.nextLine()` throws `NoSuchElementException`, which nothing catches, and the program crashes, but the files were already written.

- *Only option 7 saves*: option 7 saves too, but every successful change already did.
- *The crash rolls the file back*: plain file writes have no rollback.
- *A finally block*: `run()` has none; the save happened earlier, inside `deposit`.

notes.title: Why an edited balance is believed
notes.body:
The balance is stored as its own field. `loadAccounts` builds each `BankAccount` with `new BigDecimal(fields.get(2))`, and the `BankService` constructor just puts the loaded accounts in a map and the loaded transactions in a list. Nothing adds up the history or compares it with the balance, so the list shows **Balance: $500.00**.

- *Rebuilt from transactions*: no code derives a balance from records.
- *A mismatch error*: no consistency check exists.
- *$505.00*: transactions are never replayed onto a balance at load time.

This is a design choice worth noticing: the history is a log, not the source of truth.

notes.title: How escaping keeps a | inside a name
notes.body:
Before joining fields with `|`, `saveAccounts` runs each value through `escape`, which writes a backslash as two backslashes and `|` as backslash-pipe. The line holds **Al\|ice**. On load, `splitLine` reads character by character: after a backslash it appends the next character as plain text, and only an unescaped `|` ends a field. The record still has 4 fields and the name comes back as **Al|ice**.

- *Stored raw, load fails*: that is what would happen without `escape`.
- *Stored as Alice*: nothing strips characters.
- *Loads back as Al*: the escaped pipe is not treated as a separator.

excerpts.quote: } else if (currentChar == '\\') { escaping = true; } else if (currentChar == '|') {

notes.title: Why a non-numeric balance crashes startup
notes.body:
`loadAccounts` calls `new BigDecimal(fields.get(2))`. For `abc` that throws `NumberFormatException`, an unchecked exception. `main` only has `catch (IOException exception)`, so the exception escapes and the JVM prints a **stack trace**.

- *"Failed to load or save bank data:"*: printed only for an `IOException`, such as the "Invalid account record" thrown for a wrong number of fields.
- *Loads as 0.00*: there is no default for a bad balance.
- *Skipped*: the loader has no per-line error handling.

excerpts.quote: } catch (IOException exception) { System.out.println("Failed to load or save bank data: " + exception.getMessage());

notes.title: Why a refused transfer leaves no trace
notes.body:
`transfer` runs all of its checks before it changes anything. The balance check `sourceAccount.getBalance().compareTo(cleanAmount) < 0` throws `IllegalStateException` while both balances are untouched and before any `Transaction` is created. `App.transfer` never reaches its `saveData()` call, and `run()` prints "Operation failed: Insufficient balance for this transfer." **Nothing changes**, in memory or on disk.

- *A failed TRANSFER_OUT record*: records are created only after the money moves.
- *Overdraw to -1.00*: overdrafts are exactly what the check forbids.
- *Partial transfer of 30.00*: the code never moves less than the amount asked.

excerpts.quote: if (sourceAccount.getBalance().compareTo(cleanAmount) < 0) { throw new IllegalStateException("Insufficient balance for this transfer."); } sourceAccount.decreaseBalance(cleanAmount);
